name: September 2026 · International · Version 3 · Reading & Writing
description: Full-length SAT Reading & Writing from the September 2026 exam · 2 modules × 27 = 54 questions. 27 questions that could not be read from the source scan are filled in from the Humo AI question bank.

questions.passage: The following text is adapted from Zora Neale Hurston’s 1921 short story “John Redding Goes to Sea.” John wants to travel far beyond the village where he lives near his mother, Matty. [John] had on several occasions attempted to reconcile his mother to the notion, but found it a difficult task. Matty always took refuge in self-pity and tears. Her son’s desires were incomprehensible to her, that was all.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does the phrase “reconcile his mother to” most nearly mean?
options: Get his mother to accept
Get his mother to apologize for
Get his mother to match
Get his mother to reunite with
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A.

questions.passage: The following text is adapted from Karel Č apek’s 1920 play R.U.R. (Rossum’s Universal Robots ), translated by Paul Selver and Nigel Playfair in 1923. Fabry and Busman are telling Miss Glory why their company manufactures robots. FABRY: One Robot can replace two and a half workmen. The human machine, Miss Glory, was terribly imperfect. It had to be removed sooner or later. BUSMAN: It was too expensive. FABRY: It was not effective. It no longer answers the requirements of modern engineering. Nature has no idea of keeping pace with modern labor.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does the word “answers” most nearly mean?
options: Explains
Rebuts
Defends
Fulfills
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D.

questions.passage: Navigators in the Marshall Islands once built charts from strips of palm rib lashed together, with small shells marking the positions of islands. The charts depicted not coastlines but the patterns that ocean swells form as they bend around land. Historian Lani Kabua argues that European visitors who dismissed the charts as crude misunderstood them: the charts were not unsuccessful versions of the maps Europeans drew but instruments of an altogether different order, meant to be studied and memorized on shore rather than consulted during a voyage.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does the word "order" most nearly mean?
options: command
sequence
kind
arrangement
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C.

questions.passage:
Text 1
When the printing press spread across Europe in the late 1400s, books could be produced far faster and more cheaply than before. Historian Ilse Brandt credits the press with helping new scientific ideas reach readers in many countries, speeding the exchange of knowledge.

Text 2
The printing press did not spread only accurate information. Historian Rafael Ortiz points out that printers also turned out large numbers of pamphlets full of rumors and false accusations, because such material sold well. In Ortiz's view, the press made it easier for all kinds of ideas, true and false, to circulate.
questions.question: Based on the texts, Brandt (Text 1) and Ortiz (Text 2) would most likely agree with which statement?
options: The printing press slowed the exchange of ideas between countries.
The printing press was used mainly to publish scientific works.
The printing press allowed written material to reach many more readers than before.
Most pamphlets produced by early printers contained accurate information.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C.

questions.passage:
Text 1
In Hindustani classical music of northern India, many ragas (melodic frameworks) are traditionally assigned to particular times of day—some to dawn, others to late night. Musicologist Arjun Mehta argues that these assignments should be respected because they connect each raga to the mood of its hour and are an essential part of the tradition.

Text 2
Concert organizer Kavita Rao notes that most public concerts today take place in the evening, when audiences are free. If performers followed the time-of-day rules strictly, she observes, morning ragas would almost never be heard in concert halls. Rao suggests that performers sometimes play morning ragas in the evening so that audiences can still experience them.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would Rao (Text 2) most likely respond to Mehta's argument in Text 1?
options: She would suggest that following the time-of-day rules strictly could keep audiences from hearing some ragas.
She would argue that ragas are not actually linked to particular times of day.
She would agree that morning ragas should never be performed in the evening.
She would claim that most concerts in northern India take place in the morning.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A.

questions.passage:
Text 1
In ninth-century Baghdad, the ruling caliphs paid scholars to translate scientific and philosophical works from Greek into Arabic. A common account describes these scholars mainly as preservers: they kept ancient Greek knowledge safe until European scholars rediscovered it centuries later.

Text 2
Historian Farid Navabi has compared Arabic translations of Greek astronomy books with the original Greek texts. The Arabic versions, he found, often correct errors in the Greek tables of star positions, using new observations made by astronomers in Baghdad. Translators also added long commentaries that disagreed with the Greek authors and proposed new methods for calculating the movements of planets.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would Navabi most likely respond to the common account described in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that the Baghdad scholars copied Greek works without making changes
By arguing that the Greek texts were translated into Arabic only after Europeans rediscovered them
By claiming that astronomers in Baghdad did not study Greek works at all
By arguing that the account underestimates the original contributions the Baghdad scholars made
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D.

questions.passage:
Text 1 A tiny, unusual fossil in a piece of 99-million-year-old amber is of the extinct species Oculudentavis khaungraae. The O. khaungraae fossil consists of a rounded skull with a thin snout and a large eye socket. Because these features look like they are avian, or related to birds, researchers initially thought that the fossil might be the smallest avian dinosaur ever found.

Text 2 Paleontologists were excited to discover a second small fossil that is similar to the strange O. khaungraae fossil but has part of the lower body along with a birdlike skull. Detailed studies of both fossils revealed several traits that are found in lizards but not in dinosaurs or birds. Therefore, paleontologists think the two creatures were probably unusual lizards, even though the skulls looked avian at first.
questions.question: Based on the texts, what would the paleontologists in Text 2 most likely say about the researchers’ initial thought in Text 1?
options: It is understandable because the fossil does look like it could be related to birds, even though O. khaungraae is probably a lizard.
It is confusing because it isn’t clear what caused the researchers to think that O. khaungraae might be related to birds.
It is flawed because the researchers mistakenly assumed that O. khaungraae must be a lizard.
It is reasonable because the O. khaungraae skull is about the same size as the skull of the second fossil but is shaped differently.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Spider silk is tougher, weight for weight, than steel, but spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms. Materials scientist Henrik Dahl's team inserted spider silk genes into bacteria, which then produced silk proteins. When the team drew these proteins into fibers, the fibers were only about a third as strong as natural silk. Dahl concludes that the bacterially produced proteins must differ in some important way from the proteins spiders make.

Text 2
Materials scientist Ayumi Kobayashi notes that a spider does not simply squeeze silk out of its body. As silk proteins flow through the spider's gland, they are exposed to gradually increasing acidity and are stretched, which lines the protein chains up. Kobayashi's team took bacterially produced silk proteins and passed them through a narrow channel that mimicked these conditions. The resulting fibers were nearly as strong as natural silk.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would Kobayashi most likely respond to Dahl's conclusion?
options: She would agree that bacteria are unable to produce spider silk proteins.
She would argue that the weakness of Dahl's fibers may reflect how the proteins were spun rather than a difference in the proteins themselves.
She would claim that natural spider silk is actually weaker than steel.
She would suggest that Dahl's fibers were weak because his bacteria were exposed to too much acidity.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B.

questions.passage:
Text 1 The fossil record suggests that mammoths went extinct around 11 thousand years (kyr) ago. In a 2021 study of environmental DNA (eDNA)—genetic material shed into the environment by organisms—in the Arctic, Yucheng Wang and colleagues found mammoth eDNA in sedimentary layers formed millennia later, around 4 kyr ago. To account for this discrepancy, Joshua H. Miller and Carl Simpson proposed that arctic temperatures could preserve a mammoth carcass on the surface, allowing it to leach DNA into the environment, for several thousand years.

Text 2 Wang and colleagues concede that eDNA contains DNA from both living organisms and carcasses, but for DNA to leach from remains over several millennia requires that the remains be perpetually on the surface. Scavengers and weathering in the Arctic, however, are likely to break down surface remains well before a thousand years have passed.
questions.question: Which choice best describes how Text 1 and Text 2 relate to each other?
options: Text 1 discusses two approaches to studying mammoth extinction without advocating for either, whereas Text 2 advocates for one approach over the other.

Text 1 presents findings by Wang and colleagues and gives another research team’s attempt to explain those findings, whereas Text 2 provides additional detail that calls that explanation into question.
Text 1 describes Wang and colleagues’ study and a critique of their methodology, whereas Text 2 offers additional details showing that methodology to be sound.
Text 1 argues that new research has undermined the standard view of when mammoths went extinct, whereas Text 2 suggests a way to reconcile the standard view with that new research.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B.

questions.passage:
Text 1
So-called Damascus blades, forged in Syrian workshops from ingots of wootz steel imported from southern India, were prized for their wavy surface patterns and their toughness. Using electron microscopes, materials scientist Rania Haddad found carbon nanotubes and nanowires of iron carbide inside several such blades. Because these structures arise only under a demanding sequence of heating, hammering, and cooling, Haddad argues that the smiths deliberately engineered them through their closely guarded forging methods, displaying a sophisticated, if untheorized, control over their material.

Text 2
Metallurgist Vikram Sethi has reproduced patterned wootz blades in the laboratory. He confirms that the traditional forging sequence is required to bring out the nanostructures. But the structures formed only when the steel contained tiny traces of vanadium, an impurity present in ore from a few Indian deposits. Historical sources indicate that when those deposits were exhausted in the eighteenth century, the patterns vanished from new blades even though smiths continued to follow the same forging methods, and the methods were eventually lost.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would Sethi most likely respond to Haddad's argument?
options: He would argue that the nanostructures in the blades formed through corrosion long after the blades were forged.
He would argue that the smiths' forging methods played no role in producing the nanostructures.
He would grant that the forging methods were necessary but argue that the smiths' success depended on a property of their raw material that their methods did not control.
He would claim that the smiths deliberately added vanadium to their steel in order to create the blades' patterns.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C.

questions.passage: The following text is adapted from Robert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 novel Treasure Island. Bill is a sailor staying at the Admiral Benbow, an inn run by the narrator’s parents. Every day when [Bill] came back from his stroll he would ask if any seafaring men had gone by along the road. At first we thought it was the want of company of his own kind that made him ask this question, but at last we began to see he was desirous to avoid them. When a seaman did [stay] at the Admiral Benbow (as now and then some did) he would look in at him through the curtained door before he entered the parlour; and he was always sure to be as silent as a mouse when any such was present.
questions.question: According to the text, why does Bill regularly ask about “seafaring men”?
options: He’s hoping to find an old friend and fellow sailor.
He’s trying to secure a job as part of the crew on a new ship.
He isn’t sure that other guests at the inn will be welcoming of sailors.
He doesn’t want to encounter any other sailor unexpectedly.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D.

questions.passage: In many of his sculptures, artist Richard Hunt uses broad forms rather than extreme accuracy to hint at specific people or ideas. In his first major work, Arachne (1956), Hunt constructed the mythical character Arachne, a weaver who was changed into a spider, by welding bits of steel together into something that, although vaguely human, is strange and machine-like. And his large bronze sculpture The Light of Truth (2021) commemorates activist and journalist Ida B. Wells using mainly flowing, curved pieces of metal that create stylized flame.
questions.question: Which choice best states the text’s main idea about Hunt?
options: He often depicts the subjects of his sculptures using an unrealistic style.
He uses different kinds of materials depending on what kind of sculpture he plans to create.
He tends to base his art on important historical figures rather than on fictional characters.
He has altered his approach to sculpture over time, and his works have become increasingly abstract.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A.

questions.passage: To protect themselves when being attacked, hagfish— jawless marine animals that resemble eels—will release large quantities of slimy, mucus-like threads. Because these threads are unusually strong and elastic, scientist Atsuko Negishi and her colleagues have been trying to recreate them in a lab as an eco-friendly alternative to petroleum-based fibers that are often used in fabrics. The researchers want to reproduce the threads in the lab because farming hagfish for their slime would be expensive and potentially harmful to the hagfish.
questions.question: Which choice best states the text’s main idea?
options: The slimy threads that hagfish release might help researchers create a new kind of fabric.
Hagfish have inspired researchers to develop a new petroleum-based fabric.
Hagfish are not well suited to being raised in captivity.
The ability of hagfish to slime their attackers compensates for their being jawless.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A.

questions.passage: Insecticide-treated bed nets reduce malaria by preventing mosquito bites during sleep. In a district of Tanzania, public health researcher Neema Mushi observed that after nets were widely distributed, malaria cases fell sharply among young children but much less among adults. One explanation is that adults were less likely to use the nets. But household surveys showed that adults and children slept under nets at nearly identical rates. Mushi instead noticed that many adults in the district spent evenings outdoors—cooking, socializing, or working—during hours when local mosquitoes had begun to bite, while young children were typically put to bed early. She proposes that the nets protected adults during sleep about as well as they protected children, but that adults received many bites during waking hours, when no net could help.
questions.question: According to the text, why does Mushi reject the explanation that adults were less likely to use the nets?
options: Adults were found to spend more evening hours outdoors than children did.
Malaria cases among adults did not fall at all after the nets were distributed.
Surveys indicated that adults used the nets at about the same rate as children.
Local mosquitoes were found to bite mainly during the hours when people sleep.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C.

questions.passage: In 1967 the US Congress created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which in turn created National Public Radio (NPR). NPR began producing and distributing high-quality news and cultural programming to affiliate stations across the United States in 1971. In a research paper, a student claims that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and NPR were inspired by the British Broadcasting System (BBC), which had been established in the 1920s.
questions.question: Which quotation from a work by a historian would be the most effective evidence for the student to include in support of this claim?
options: “Although the BBC had begun as a private corporation, politicians successfully argued to make it a public company because they believed a public broadcaster could help build national unity in the aftermath of World War I.”

“For many decades, the BBC had no competition since it held Britain’s only broadcasting license, whereas in the United States, the Corporation for Public Broadcasting launched NPR in a broadcasting market already filled with competitors.”

“Congress’s embrace of publicly funded broadcasting reflected a common belief among US politicians that the role of government was not only to ensure people’s safety and liberty but also to enrich people’s lives in other ways.”

“The goal of the BBC was to support British democracy by promoting an informed citizenry, and US legislators believed that ensuring access to high-quality programming could do the same for democracy in the United States.”
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D.

questions.passage: In the seventeenth century, Ottoman authorities repeatedly ordered the coffeehouses of Istanbul closed. Some historians attribute these bans to religious objections to coffee itself, which certain scholars of the period condemned as an intoxicant. Historian Cemal Yıldırımlı rejects that view. In his account, the authorities were not troubled by coffee as a substance at all; what they feared was the political conversation that flourished wherever men gathered to drink it in public. The bans, he argues, therefore targeted the institution of the coffeehouse rather than the beverage, and should be read as instruments of political surveillance rather than of religious discipline.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Yıldırımlı's argument over the view he rejects?
options: Religious scholars of the period produced treatises both condemning coffee and defending it as permissible.
Each ban was widely ignored, and many coffeehouses reopened within a few months of being closed.
Several of the edicts announcing the bans cited the "idle and seditious talk" heard in coffeehouses alongside claims that coffee harms the body.
The edicts ordered coffeehouses shut but placed no restriction on the sale of coffee beans, and coffee imports into Istanbul did not decline during the years of the bans.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D.

questions.passage: The interiors of many temples in the ancient Middle East needed to satisfy a precise set of acoustic demands: the sounds of chants and hymns should travel with clarity, while profound silences should be fully felt and appreciated. In a research paper, a student claims that the users of one such temple were aware of how the materials that were used within the structure could affect sound quality and that they deliberately applied this knowledge to influence how sound was experienced in the space.
questions.question: Which quotation from a work by a historian would most directly support the student’s claim?
options: “Many researchers believe that the central chamber of the temple had a high ceiling, a feature that has since become essential to the acoustic design of modern concert halls.”
“The innermost room of the temple was likely among the quietest spaces in the interior of the temple.”
“The acoustic environment of the temple was best suited for music that eschewed ornamentation in favor of simple melodies, harmonies, and rhythms.”
“During special occasions, curtains were placed inside the temple to minimize reverberation and confine the sound to designated locations.”
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D.

questions.passage: Nigerian novelist Chidinma Okafor writes most of her narration in standard English, but her characters often speak in Nigerian Pidgin, a language widely used across the country's many ethnic groups. Okafor has said that she does not translate or explain her characters' Pidgin for readers outside Nigeria. She wants the dialogue to sound the way people in Lagos actually talk, and she trusts readers to understand meaning from context, as they would if they were visiting the city themselves.
questions.question: Based on the text, why does Okafor not translate her characters' Pidgin?
options: She intends her novels to be read only by people who live in Nigeria.
She believes that Nigerian Pidgin cannot be translated into English.
She wants the dialogue to sound authentic and believes readers can grasp its meaning from context.
Her publishers require her to keep explanations out of her novels.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Mama Ronke has sold fabric at the same stall in a Lagos market for decades.

Customers who came to Mama Ronke hoping for a bargain left disappointed; she did not lower her prices, not even for regulars. Yet the stall was never empty. Young women about to marry came to her not for the cloth alone but for her verdict—whether the green would flatter, whether the pattern was too loud for a mother-in-law's house. She gave these opinions freely and bluntly, and more than one bride had walked away with a cheaper fabric from another stall because Mama Ronke had told her it suited her better.
questions.question: Based on the text, why do customers keep coming to Mama Ronke's stall?
options: She offers the lowest prices of any seller in the market.
They value her frank advice, which she gives even when it costs her a sale.
Custom requires brides to buy their fabric from the oldest seller in the market.
She rewards loyal customers by lowering her prices for them.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B.

questions.passage:

enmity
anomaly
ambiguity

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Yone Noguchi’s 1914 memoir The Story of Yone Noguchi. Noguchi is returning home after eleven years abroad.

I reached Tsushima, my native town, at evening.

I frightened my old father at the station, who was actually trying to find me among some other people. There is no wonder that he could not recognise me; I must have changed a great deal.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does the word “find” most nearly mean?
options: Locate
Reveal
Persuade
Embarrass
questions.explanation: His father was trying to spot, or locate, him among the crowd.

questions.passage: In addition to the giant stock exchanges in places like London, Mumbai, and Tokyo, there are many smaller exchanges such as the Beirut Stock Exchange in Beirut, Lebanon. Though small, by being dedicated to Lebanon, it can better address factors that help local businesses ______, and that focus on the success of local businesses benefits investors and the local economy.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: thrive
disperse
ebb
overspend
questions.explanation: Factors that help businesses and benefit the economy help them “thrive.”

questions.passage: Researchers César A. Hidalgo, Elisa Castañer, and Andres Sevtsuk created a computer model to predict the mix of movie theaters, gyms, and other businesses found in a given neighborhood. How we define a neighborhood and its boundaries is subjective, so the team used a clustering algorithm to locate dense groupings of amenities that represent human-identified neighborhoods like Boston’s Harvard Square. The predictive model, which incorporates this algorithm, is sure to be invaluable in determining the optimal mix of a city’s amenities.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It praises an algorithm’s accuracy in identifying neighborhood boundaries.
It emphasizes the potential utility of the team’s model.
It suggests a difficulty associated with analyzing neighborhoods that the research team attempted to overcome.
It summarizes trends in recent urban development in Boston.
questions.explanation: The sentence says the model will be “invaluable,” which stresses its potential usefulness.

questions.passage: Asteroid 6478 Gault has experienced intermittent mass loss since at least 2013, but in contrast to some other asteroids with repeated mass-loss episodes, 6478 Gault has not lost mass at its perihelion (the closest point of its orbit to the Sun), and thus the loss is not attributable to solar energy-driven ice vaporization. And as Jane X. Luu et al. point out, the singular nature of impact ejection makes it untenable as an account of multiple loss episodes of similar duration over several years. Instead, Luu et al. are likely correct that 6478 Gault is shedding mass due to rotational instability.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a scientific observation, describes a contrast between that observation and other observations, and then explains why those other observations should not be considered credible.
It describes an astronomical finding, discusses competing theories about that finding that the author regards as flawed, and then describes new evidence that supports an alternative theory.
It discusses a physical process, evaluates possible causes of that process, and then states that a persuasive account of the process has yet to be put forward.
It introduces a natural phenomenon, refutes two potential explanations for that phenomenon, and then presents a third explanation for that phenomenon that the author regards as plausible.
questions.explanation: The text rules out ice vaporization and impact ejection, then favors rotational instability.

questions.passage: Community science, which involves professional scientists collaborating with amateur science enthusiasts to study a topic, is often an effective and engaging way to conduct research. It can allow people to assist with conservation efforts, provide youth with learning experiences outside of the classroom, and increase the amount of data researchers can collect. This approach was essential to the success of a study by biologist Grace Herzel and colleagues of butterfly color and its relation to behavior, which included findings from hundreds of students and community members in northwestern Arkansas.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It argues for a new approach to scientific research, comments on the public’s opinion about the approach, and then describes how that approach was applied in a certain study.
It introduces the topic of a scientific study, describes the study’s importance, and then presents the study’s results.
It describes the development of a type of scientific collaboration, shows how that type of collaboration has been used in a particular field of study, and then suggests future collaborative projects.
It identifies a particular approach to research, lists some benefits of that approach, and then mentions a study in which that approach was used.
questions.explanation: The text names community science, lists its benefits, and then cites the Herzel study.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Death Cab for Cutie’s 2003 song “Lightness” includes a specific musical pattern. That pattern consists of two alternating notes sung over and over with “wa” and “oh” sounds, resulting in a sequence of “Wa-oh-wa-oh.” This pattern showed up in so many pop songs in the 2000s and 2010s that eventually it earned a nickname, “the millennial whoop.” Unfortunately, the whoop showed up so frequently that it could be more irritating than enjoyable.

Text 2

The millennial whoop could be annoying. Not every pop song needs “Wa-oh-wa-ohs!” and it seemed as though nearly every pop song released between 2000 and 2017 had them. But the whoop could also be genuinely fun or even moving. Too many songwriters used it in too many pop songs for a time, but that doesn’t mean the whoop was never used well.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the relationship between the perspectives provided in Text 1 and Text 2?
options: Text 1 provides an explanation of events that inspired a song, while Text 2 offers a different explanation of those events.
Text 1 discusses the advantages of a technique for recording music, while Text 2 discusses the problems with that technique.
Text 1 introduces a negative view of a musical pattern, while Text 2 presents a more positive view of that pattern.
Text 1 focuses on critics who praised a particular style of music, while Text 2 focuses on critics who disapproved of that style.
questions.explanation: Text 1 calls the whoop irritating; Text 2 admits it was overused but says it could be fun or moving.

questions.passage: Why do flat-headed cats purr but jaguars roar? Researchers hypothesize that this difference between the two feline species may be partly due to a U-shaped bone in their throats called the hyoid. Flat-headed cats, which are much smaller than jaguars, have a rigid hyoid that rumbles when the cat’s larynx vibrates, resulting in a purr. By contrast, jaguars have a somewhat flexible hyoid, and the bone is attached to the skull with a stretchy ligament that flat-headed cats lack. These traits allow jaguars and most other species of big cats to produce powerful roars. The same traits may also prevent most big cats from purring.
questions.question: According to the text, which trait do researchers think may contribute to a flat-headed cat’s ability to purr?
options: The shape of the flat-headed cat’s larynx
The ligament attaching the hyoid bone to the flat-headed cat’s skull
The flat-headed cat’s rigid hyoid bone
The relative size of the flat-headed cat’s body and throat
questions.explanation: The text says a rigid hyoid rumbles when the larynx vibrates, producing a purr.

questions.passage: Memoirs of Elleanor Eldridge is an 1838 historical account by Elleanor Eldridge and Frances Harriet Whipple Green. In the book, the authors assert that people don’t need to be famous to be worthy of memoirs, writing,
questions.question: Which quotation from Memoirs of Elleanor Eldridge most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Then let no one turn with too much [fussiness] from the simple story of the humble Elleanor, though it may contain few, or none, of the thrilling charms of poetry and passion.”

“There is often a kind of [deceptive] light, playing around such [famous] names, calculated to dazzle and mislead, by their false lustre, until the eye can no longer receive the pure light of Truth, or the mind appreciate real excellence, or intrinsic worth.”
“It should not be considered essential to the interest and value of biography, that its subject be of exalted rank, or illustrious name.”

“How careful ought we to be to speak nothing but the truth, even in regard to the most trifling circumstances; and not only so, but to be well assured that what we suppose to be true, is truth, before we receive it as such.”
questions.explanation: Only C says a subject need not have exalted rank or an illustrious name to be worth a biography.

questions.passage: A student is writing a research paper on the history of irrigation in the United States, situating the development of the Bear River Reservoir (created in Amador County, California, in 1900) in a larger historical context. The student claims that innovation in irrigation practices throughout the United States has led to designs with increased efficiency.
questions.question: Which quotation from a study of irrigation best supports the student’s claim?
options: “While the low humidity of Southern California’s desert areas makes irrigation a requirement if agriculture is to be a success there, the relatively high humidity in the northern parts of the state makes such practices less necessary.”

“The importance of irrigation infrastructure in the United States today cannot be overstated, since it is the most widely utilized means of conveying water for food production. Accordingly, any increase in the efficiency of irrigation, however small, would be of significant economic and social value.”
“The irrigation system developed by the Hohokam people in the 7th century CE in what is now Arizona was simple but applied hydraulic engineering design features that are still in use today.”

“Competition for water as a scarce economic resource inspired the development of sprinkler irrigation systems, which have contributed to the reduction of water used for irrigation in the United States to 45% of the total water usage of its population. Comparatively, 70% of the world’s water usage is dedicated to irrigation.”
questions.explanation: Only D describes an innovation (sprinkler systems) that made irrigation more efficient by reducing the water used.

questions.passage: Studying animals in a laboratory allows variables to be systematically controlled, but removing animals from their wild habitats can affect their behavior and biology in unforeseen ways. Given this, biologists Rebecca M. Calisi-Rodriguez and George E. Bentley examined research on brown-throated three-toed sloths and canaries to see whether results from studies in the wild were consistent with the results of studies in the laboratory. Therefore, data showing that brown-throated three-toed sloths tend to sleep fewer than 10 hours per day in the wild would be irrelevant to Calisi-Rodriguez and Bentley’s investigation if ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: this behavior pattern has not been studied in the lab.
they tend to sleep more than 15 hours per day in the lab.
the brains of male canaries show predictable seasonal changes in the wild.
such data have been collected for canaries in laboratory settings but not in the wild.
questions.explanation: Wild data can only be compared with lab data if the lab data exist; without lab studies of sloth sleep, the wild data would be irrelevant to the comparison.

questions.passage: Carl Woese’s 1970s study of methanogens (microbes with no nuclei, such as Methanococcus vannielii, that metabolize hydrogen and carbon dioxide in oxygen-poor environments and produce methane as a by-product) suggested that they did not fit scientists’ then-conventional division of life into two domains, the eukaryotes (having cells with nuclei) and the prokaryotes (missing nuclei). Molecular clock evidence indicated that what Woese argued was a third domain of life emerged as early as 3.5 billion years ago. Methanogens would have been well-adapted to conditions then given that ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: atmospheric hydrogen levels were much lower around 3.3 billion years ago than they were both earlier and later in Earth’s history.
methane, while primarily biological in origin on Earth, can be produced in the absence of biological activity.
the earliest undisputed evidence of eukaryotes is much more recent than 3.5 billion years ago.
Earth’s oxygen levels were very low until the Great Oxidation Event approximately 2.4 billion years ago.
questions.explanation: Methanogens thrive in oxygen-poor environments, and Earth had very little oxygen until about 2.4 billion years ago, so they were well suited to early Earth.

questions.passage: The Southern Delta Aquariid meteor shower has a zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) of 25, meaning that at the shower’s peak, 25 meteors per hour could potentially be seen by a hypothetical observer. A calculation that assumes ideal viewing conditions, ______
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: an actual viewer’s observed number of meteors in an hour and the ZHR may differ considerably.
the number of meteors an actual viewer observes in an hour may differ considerably from the ZHR.
there may be a considerable difference between the number of meteors an actual viewer observes in an hour and the ZHR.
the ZHR may differ considerably from the number of meteors an actual viewer observes in an hour.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase “A calculation that assumes ideal viewing conditions” describes the ZHR, so “the ZHR” must come next.

questions.passage: Jordan’s constitution, enacted in 1952, contains just one of the six constitutional features that enhance judicial independence, as identified by legal scholars James Melton and Tom Ginsburg. containing
had contained
contains

questions.passage: Many Farms Chapter, which covers 168,000 acres, is one of the 110 chapters of the Navajo ______ Diné bizaad (the Navajo language), the chapter is called Da’ak’eh Halani.

Nation. In
Nation and in
Nation in

Dellums, who represented California in the United States House of Representatives, the student discovered biographical sketches of two other Black Americans who served in ______ Ralph Harold Metcalfe of Illinois and George Henry White of North Carolina.

Congress:
Congress;
Congress

At last,
For example,

Periodically,
Accordingly,

Finally,
Similarly,
Therefore,

in turn,
specifically,
for example,

questions.passage: For several centuries after the birth of opera in sixteenth-century Florence, Italian remained the default language in which most opera scores were written. ______ opera singers today, such as the tenor Lawrence Brownlee, encounter a wide range of Italian terms—from affettuoso (with feeling) to affrettando (at a hurried tempo)—when following many eighteenth-century opera scores.

Lastly,
Granted,
However,

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Leidenfrost effect occurs when liquid touches a solid surface significantly hotter than the liquid’s boiling point, forming a vapor layer that insulates the liquid before eventually collapsing.
  • Scientists long hypothesized that the temperatures at which Leidenfrost vapor forms and collapses vary depending on molecular variations in surfaces and liquids.
  • A 2023 study confirmed that the vapor’s formation temperature varies depending on molecular variations in surfaces and liquids.
  • The study also found that the vapor’s collapse temperature was “nearly independent of material and fluid properties,” contrary to previous theories.
  • The vapor’s collapse temperature remained consistent (around 140°C).
questions.question: The student wants to refute a scientific assumption about the Leidenfrost effect. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Though the vapor layer created by the Leidenfrost effect can be formed at a range of temperatures, the temperature at which the layer collapses varies depending on material and fluid properties.

Scientists had hypothesized that the formation temperature of Leidenfrost vapor depends on variations in surfaces and liquids used, but a 2023 study confirmed that the collapse temperature remains consistent.
Countering previous hypotheses, a recent study found that Leidenfrost vapor’s collapse temperature does not vary depending on material and fluid properties.

Contrary to the hypothesis that vapor layer formation temperature is dictated by molecular variation, a 2023 study confirmed that the temperature at which the vapor layer forms depends on the surface and liquid used.
questions.explanation: The assumption that collapse temperature varies with materials is refuted by the finding that it does not; C states this directly.

options: Both the Crocodile Lake NWR and the Pearl Harbor NWR were established to protect endangered species.
Some NWRs, such as Hawaii’s Pearl Harbor, were established specifically to protect endangered species.
While the Crocodile Lake NWR extends across a 6,686-acre area, the Pearl Harbor NWR encompasses only 61 acres.
The US has designated more than 500 areas as NWRs, including the Crocodile Lake NWR in Florida.

options: Rodinia and Euramerica were both supercontinents, single landmasses made up of most or all of the Earth’s continents.
Rodinia formed about 1.1 billion years ago, long before Euramerica’s formation about 300 million years ago.
Forming and breaking apart over hundreds of millions of years, supercontinents are made up of most or all of Earth’s continents.
Euramerica and Rodinia formed at different times in Earth’s history.
